questions.body: In Java, what happens if a subclass attempts to override a protected method of its superclass and declare it as package-private (no modifier)?
questions.keyPoints: Method overriding cannot reduce the visibility of inherited methods.

options.text: A compilation error occurs because an overriding method cannot assign weaker access privileges than the overridden method.
options.explanation: Java enforces that an overriding method cannot reduce visibility (protected to default/package-private reduces access, which is forbidden).

options.text: The code compiles successfully, but throws an IllegalAccessException at runtime during dynamic dispatch.
options.explanation: Access privilege rules are strictly enforced at compile time in Java.

options.text: The method is treated as method overloading rather than method overriding.
options.explanation: Matching signature with incompatible access privilege is an invalid override, not overloading.

options.text: The compiler allows it only if the subclass is in the exact same package as the superclass.
options.explanation: Even within the same package, an override cannot reduce visibility from protected to package-private.

questions.body: A superclass declares `public Number getVal()`. A subclass overrides this method with `public Integer getVal()`. Which of the following is true?
questions.keyPoints: Java allows covariant return types in method overriding since Java 5.

options.text: It compiles successfully because Java allows covariant return types where the return type is a subtype of the superclass method's return type.
options.explanation: Since Java 5, an overriding method is allowed to return a more specific subtype (Integer is a subtype of Number).

options.text: It fails to compile because method overriding requires an identical return type signature.
options.explanation: Subtypes are permitted as return types (covariant returns).

options.text: It compiles, but causes runtime ClassCastException when invoked via a superclass reference.
options.explanation: Polymorphic invocation returns the Integer, which is a valid Number reference.

options.text: It requires the `@Covariant` annotation to compile without warnings.
options.explanation: There is no `@Covariant` annotation in Java.

questions.body: If class `C` implements interfaces `A` and `B`, and both interfaces provide conflicting default implementations for `void execute()`, what must class `C` do to compile?
questions.keyPoints: Conflicting default methods require explicit override in the implementing class.

options.text: Class C must explicitly override execute() and resolve the ambiguity (e.g. by providing its own implementation or calling A.super.execute()).
options.explanation: When two implemented interfaces declare default methods with the exact same signature, the compiler forces the implementing class to explicitly override it.

options.text: Class C inherits the implementation from the first interface listed in its implements clause (A).
options.explanation: Java does not resolve default method conflicts based on interface ordering.

options.text: Class C cannot implement both interfaces; the combination is rejected by the compiler.
options.explanation: A class can implement both as long as it overrides the conflicting method.

options.text: Class C automatically inherits an empty no-op implementation.
options.explanation: The compiler issues an ambiguity error if not explicitly resolved.

questions.body: What is a primary architectural reason to prefer an abstract class over an interface in Java 8+?
questions.keyPoints: Abstract classes can hold non-static mutable state and constructors, whereas interfaces cannot.

options.text: When you need to define instance state (non-static, mutable fields) or define constructors that enforce state initialization.
options.explanation: Interfaces can only have public static final constants and cannot define constructors or instance state.

options.text: When you need to provide default method implementations.
options.explanation: Interfaces have supported default methods since Java 8.

options.text: When you need static helper methods.
options.explanation: Interfaces have supported static methods since Java 8.

options.text: When you need multiple inheritance of type definitions.
options.explanation: A class can implement multiple interfaces, but can extend only one abstract class.

questions.body: What happens when a subclass defines a `static` method with the exact same name and parameter signature as a `static` method in its superclass?
questions.keyPoints: Static methods are hidden, not overridden; dispatch is determined by reference type at compile time.

options.text: The subclass hides the superclass static method; invocation is resolved at compile time based on the reference type.
options.explanation: Static methods cannot be overridden polymorphically. They are subject to method hiding, resolved at compile-time.

options.text: The subclass overrides the method polymorphically using runtime dynamic dispatch.
options.explanation: Dynamic dispatch applies only to instance methods, not static methods.

options.text: A compile-time error occurs because static methods cannot share identical signatures across an inheritance tree.
options.explanation: Method hiding is valid in Java syntax.

options.text: The superclass static method is invoked regardless of the reference type.
options.explanation: Invoking SubClass.method() runs the subclass method.

questions.body: Which of the following scenarios violates the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?
questions.keyPoints: Subclasses must be substitutable for supertypes without altering correctness or strengthening preconditions.

options.text: A subclass overrides a superclass method and throws an UnsupportedOperationException for valid inputs accepted by the superclass.
options.explanation: LSP states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. Throwing UnsupportedOperationException strengthens preconditions and breaks consumer expectations.

options.text: A subclass overrides a method to return a more specific subtype (covariant return).
options.explanation: Covariant return types satisfy LSP because any consumer expecting the base type can use the subtype.

options.text: A subclass widens the accepted input types through method overloading.
options.explanation: Overloading does not violate LSP substitutability.

options.text: A subclass overrides a method and produces the exact same side-effects with a faster algorithm.
options.explanation: Performance improvements while maintaining behavior conform to LSP.

questions.body: To build a truly immutable class containing a `java.util.Date` or `List` field, what must the constructor and getter methods do?
questions.keyPoints: Defensive copying is essential for mutable fields in immutable classes.

options.text: Perform defensive copies of the mutable object in both the constructor and the getter methods.
options.explanation: Without defensive copying, callers can mutate the internal state of the instance via external references before or after instantiation.

options.text: Declare the field as private final; no defensive copying is needed.
options.explanation: The final keyword prevents reassigning the reference, but does not prevent mutating the referenced object.

options.text: Make the class abstract so no new instances can be created.
options.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and do not solve mutability leakage.

options.text: Synchronize all getter methods.
options.explanation: Synchronization provides thread safety against concurrent execution, but does not prevent external state modification.

questions.body: If a superclass defines only one constructor with parameters `public SuperClass(int x)` and no default no-arg constructor, what must a subclass do?
questions.keyPoints: Subclass constructors must explicitly call super(param) if no default no-arg constructor exists.

options.text: Every subclass constructor must explicitly invoke super(...) on its very first statement.
options.explanation: Java automatically inserts super() as the first statement if omitted; if the superclass lacks a no-arg constructor, compilation fails unless super(...) is explicitly called.

options.text: The subclass automatically generates a default super() constructor in the superclass.
options.explanation: A superclass loses its default no-arg constructor as soon as any custom constructor is declared.

options.text: The subclass cannot be compiled unless the superclass is marked abstract.
options.explanation: Subclasses can readily extend concrete classes with parameterized constructors.

options.text: The subclass can invoke super(...) anywhere within its constructor body.
options.explanation: super(...) or this(...) must always be the very first statement in a constructor.

questions.body: Given `Animal a = new Dog();` where `Dog` extends `Animal` and overrides `speak()`, which method implementation is executed when `a.speak()` is called?
questions.keyPoints: Instance methods are resolved dynamically at runtime based on the actual object type.

options.text: Dog.speak(), because instance methods in Java use dynamic method dispatch based on the runtime instance type.
options.explanation: In Java, instance methods are virtual by default and dispatched based on the runtime type of the object (Dog).

options.text: Animal.speak(), because the variable reference type is Animal.
options.explanation: Compile-time reference types determine method accessibility, not runtime dispatch.

options.text: Both methods sequentially, starting with Animal.speak() then Dog.speak().
options.explanation: Only the overridden method is executed unless super.speak() is explicitly called inside Dog.speak().

options.text: A runtime exception occurs unless 'a' is explicitly cast to Dog.
options.explanation: No casting is necessary for polymorphic method invocation.

questions.body: Why is 'Composition over Inheritance' considered a core design guideline in object-oriented architecture?
questions.keyPoints: Composition offers loose coupling and runtime flexibility compared to fragile inheritance hierarchies.

options.text: Inheritance violates encapsulation by exposing superclass implementation details to subclasses (fragile base class problem), whereas composition creates loose coupling.
options.explanation: Composition allows behaviors to be swapped at runtime and shields components from changes in superclass internal implementation.

options.text: Inheritance cannot achieve polymorphism, whereas composition achieves polymorphism without interfaces.
options.explanation: Inheritance is one of the primary mechanisms for subtype polymorphism.

options.text: Composition uses less JVM heap memory than inheritance hierarchies.
options.explanation: Composition typically requires separate object references and allocations, which uses comparable or slightly more memory.

options.text: The Java compiler automatically converts composition into multi-inheritance at bytecode level.
options.explanation: The JVM does not support multiple class inheritance.

questions.body: In Java 17+, which modifiers must each direct subclass of a `sealed` class declare?
questions.keyPoints: Direct subclasses of a sealed class must explicitly declare final, sealed, or non-sealed.

options.text: Exactly one of: final, sealed, or non-sealed.
options.explanation: Java sealed classes require every permitted subclass to explicitly specify its own extensibility: final (cannot be extended), sealed (restricts further subclasses), or non-sealed (open for anyone to extend).

options.text: Only final is permitted for subclasses of sealed classes.
options.explanation: Subclasses can also be sealed or non-sealed.

options.text: Only static or transient.
options.explanation: These are not subclass boundary modifiers.

options.text: Subclasses do not require any special modifier if they are in the same package.
options.explanation: The compiler strictly requires one of the three modifiers even within the same compilation unit.

questions.body: Which of the following statements accurately differentiates method overloading from method overriding?
questions.keyPoints: Overloading is compile-time polymorphism with different parameter lists; overriding is runtime polymorphism with the same signature.

options.text: Overloading occurs within the same class or hierarchy with different parameter lists (compile-time); overriding occurs in a subclass with the same signature (runtime).
options.explanation: Overloading depends on the method name with different arguments and is resolved statically. Overriding has the identical signature and is resolved dynamically.

options.text: Overloading requires different return types; overriding requires identical parameter names.
options.explanation: Changing return type alone cannot overload a method; parameter names do not affect method signatures.

options.text: Overriding can only be applied to private methods.
options.explanation: Private methods cannot be overridden as they are not visible to subclasses.

options.text: Overloading cannot be used in constructors.
options.explanation: Constructor overloading is common and standard practice in Java.

questions.body: How does the Open-Closed Principle (OCP) suggest software entities should be designed?
questions.keyPoints: Classes should be open for extension, but closed for modification.

options.text: Software entities should be open for extension (e.g. via abstraction or polymorphism), but closed for modification of existing source code.
options.explanation: OCP promotes adding new features by adding new classes or implementations rather than modifying existing, tested code.

options.text: All classes must be declared public (open) and final (closed).
options.explanation: OCP is an architectural principle, not a literal keyword directive.

options.text: Open-source dependencies should be closed inside private repositories.
options.explanation: OCP is part of SOLID design principles, unrelated to source code licensing.

options.text: Methods should open database transactions and close them in a finally block.
options.explanation: This describes transaction management, not OCP.

questions.body: Which violation characterizes a failure to adhere to the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?
questions.keyPoints: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.

options.text: Clients are forced to implement fat interfaces with dummy or empty methods because they do not need the majority of operations.
options.explanation: ISP states that no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Large interfaces should be split into smaller, cohesive ones.

options.text: A class has more than one public method.
options.explanation: Having multiple cohesive methods does not violate ISP.

options.text: An interface extends more than one parent interface.
options.explanation: Interface inheritance is valid and often used to compose specific interfaces.

options.text: A class implements an interface using lambda expressions.
options.explanation: Functional interfaces and lambdas adhere to focused interface design.

questions.body: According to the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP), what should high-level modules depend upon?
questions.keyPoints: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level details.

options.text: Abstractions (interfaces or abstract classes), rather than concrete low-level implementations.
options.explanation: DIP states that high-level business logic should not depend directly on low-level utility classes; both should depend on abstractions.

options.text: Singleton concrete instances initialized statically.
options.explanation: Depending on concrete singletons increases tight coupling, violating DIP.

options.text: The underlying operating system native libraries.
options.explanation: Native dependencies introduce platform-specific tight coupling.

options.text: Subclasses created via inheritance hierarchies.
options.explanation: Superclasses should not depend on their subclasses.

questions.body: In robust software design, which combination of coupling and cohesion is desirable?
questions.keyPoints: High cohesion and low coupling produce modular, maintainable code.

options.text: High cohesion and low coupling.
options.explanation: High cohesion means a class focuses on a single well-defined purpose; low coupling means classes have minimal interdependencies.

options.text: Low cohesion and high coupling.
options.explanation: This leads to spaghetti code that is hard to test and maintain.

options.text: Low cohesion and low coupling.
options.explanation: Low cohesion results in scattered, fragmented logic across too many components.

options.text: High cohesion and high coupling.
options.explanation: High coupling makes modules tightly interdependent and difficult to reuse.

questions.keyPoints: Variables in Java are resolved at compile time using the reference type (variable shadowing, not overriding).

options.text: 10, because instance variables in Java cannot be overridden; they are resolved at compile time based on the reference type.
options.explanation: Fields are shadowed, not overridden. Accessing p.x accesses Parent.x because 'p' is typed as Parent.

options.text: 20, because polymorphic dispatch resolves instance variables to the runtime object type.
options.explanation: Polymorphic dispatch applies only to instance methods, not fields.

options.text: A compilation error occurs because a subclass cannot declare a field with the same name as its superclass.
options.explanation: Field shadowing is completely valid in Java syntax.

options.text: 0, because fields are re-initialized to default values upon subclass instantiation.
options.explanation: Parent constructor initializes Parent.x to 10.

questions.body: Which statement accurately describes `record` types introduced in Java 16+?
questions.keyPoints: Records are immutable, final data carriers with auto-generated accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString.

options.text: Records are implicitly final classes that extend java.lang.Record, and all component fields are private final.
options.explanation: Records provide concise syntax for immutable data carriers; they cannot extend other classes and their fields are private final.

options.text: Records allow extending other abstract classes as long as all fields are final.
options.explanation: Records already extend java.lang.Record and cannot extend any other class.

options.text: Records generate getter methods prefixed with 'get' (e.g. getName()).
options.explanation: Record accessor methods match the component name directly (e.g. name(), not getName()).

options.text: Records cannot implement any interfaces.
options.explanation: Records can implement any number of interfaces.

questions.keyPoints: Casting an incompatible object type at runtime throws ClassCastException.

options.text: A ClassCastException is thrown at runtime.
options.explanation: Although obj is declared as Object (so the compiler permits the cast), the actual runtime instance is a String, which cannot be cast to Integer.

options.text: A compilation error occurs at the cast expression.
options.explanation: Since Object can theoretically reference an Integer, the cast compiles.

options.text: num is assigned null without throwing any exception.
options.explanation: Java does not silently assign null on invalid explicit casts.

options.text: The string 'PathPrep' is parsed to its hash code and assigned to num.
options.explanation: Type casting does not perform data conversion or hashing.

questions.keyPoints: Pattern matching for instanceof combines type checking and binding into a single scoped variable.

options.text: It checks the type and binds the safely cast target directly to a new pattern variable in a single expression.
options.explanation: Pattern matching eliminates the boilerplate redundant explicit cast `String s = (String) obj;`.

options.text: It performs automatic reflection lookup to invoke methods dynamically.
options.explanation: Pattern matching is a static compile-time language feature, not reflection.

options.text: It permits casting between completely unrelated concrete classes at compile time.
options.explanation: The compiler still checks that the types have a potential subtype relationship.

options.text: It forces obj to be converted to a String even if it is null.
options.explanation: If obj is null, `instanceof` evaluates to false.

questions.body: Why did Java 9 introduce `private` and `private static` methods within interfaces?
questions.keyPoints: Private interface methods allow sharing code between default and static interface methods without public exposure.

options.text: To allow helper code to be shared between default or static methods in the interface without exposing it to implementing classes or callers.
options.explanation: Private interface methods prevent code duplication across multiple default methods while keeping the implementation details private to the interface.

options.text: To allow implementing classes to override private algorithms with custom logic.
options.explanation: Private methods are not visible to implementing classes and cannot be overridden.

options.text: To store confidential credentials inside compiled bytecode.
options.explanation: Bytecode can still be decompiled; private methods are for code encapsulation, not secret storage.

options.text: To replace the need for abstract classes entirely.
options.explanation: Abstract classes are still required for mutable instance state and constructors.

questions.body: What are the two design effects of marking a method and a class as `final` respectively?
questions.keyPoints: A final method cannot be overridden; a final class cannot be extended.

options.text: A final method cannot be overridden by any subclass; a final class cannot be extended by any subclass.
options.explanation: The final keyword prevents overriding on methods and prohibits inheritance on classes.

options.text: A final method can only be called once; a final class can only have one instance.
options.explanation: This confuses final with single-invocation or Singleton design patterns.

options.text: A final method cannot accept arguments; a final class cannot declare fields.
options.explanation: Final classes and methods can have parameters and fields like any other class.

options.text: A final method is always executed in a separate virtual thread.
options.explanation: The final keyword has no relationship with threading or concurrency.

questions.body: Why did Joshua Bloch and modern Java architects recommend copy constructors or static factory methods over implementing `java.lang.Cloneable`?
questions.keyPoints: Cloneable is a flawed marker interface with no public clone() method and bypasses constructors.

options.text: Cloneable is a broken marker interface that does not declare clone(), bypasses normal constructor invocation, and performs shallow copying by default.
options.explanation: Object.clone() creates an object without calling any constructor, lacks type safety, and requires complex casts and exception handling.

options.text: Cloneable causes high CPU overhead because the JVM executes it via remote native sockets.
options.explanation: Object.clone() is a fast JVM native memory copy, not a network socket call.

options.text: Cloneable requires classes to be declared final.
options.explanation: Cloneable works on non-final classes (which actually exacerbates its subtyping issues).

options.text: Cloneable was removed from Java in version 11.
options.explanation: Cloneable remains in java.lang for backward compatibility.

questions.body: What is the core definition of the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) according to Robert C. Martin?
questions.keyPoints: A class should have only one reason to change, meaning it serves a single actor or stakeholder.

options.text: A class should have only one reason to change, meaning it is responsible to only one actor or stakeholder.
options.explanation: SRP is about cohesion and change propagation: if a class handles both business logic and persistence, changes to the database structure force changes to the business logic class.

options.text: A class should contain only one method.
options.explanation: SRP does not limit classes to single methods.

options.text: A class should only be instantiated by a single thread.
options.explanation: This describes thread confinement, not SRP.

options.text: A class should have only one member field.
options.explanation: SRP is not a limitation on field counts.

questions.body: Which of the following demonstrates static (compile-time) polymorphism versus dynamic (runtime) polymorphism?
questions.keyPoints: Method overloading is static polymorphism; method overriding is dynamic polymorphism.

options.text: Method overloading is static polymorphism resolved by compiler method signatures; method overriding is dynamic polymorphism resolved via vtable lookups at runtime.
options.explanation: Overloading binds method calls at compile-time (static binding). Overriding uses virtual method tables (vtables) to resolve the implementation at runtime (dynamic binding).

options.text: Method overriding is static polymorphism; method overloading is dynamic polymorphism.
options.explanation: This reverses the definitions.

options.text: Static polymorphism requires abstract classes; dynamic polymorphism requires interfaces.
options.explanation: Both abstract classes and interfaces support dynamic polymorphism.

options.text: Static polymorphism uses Java generics; dynamic polymorphism uses Java lambdas.
options.explanation: This does not define the distinction between overloading and overriding polymorphism.
